mcqs.question: In the Dutch flag algorithm, what do the three markers low, mid, and high represent?
options: low and high are the array's fixed start and end; mid is the array's midpoint index, unchanged throughout
low counts 0s seen, mid counts 1s seen, high counts 2s seen, as running tallies
low is used only for the final output array; mid and high do all the sorting work
low and mid mark the boundary of settled 0s and 1s so far; high marks the boundary of settled 2s; mid is the current element being examined
mcqs.explanation: low/mid mark how far the settled 0s and 1s extend, high marks how far the settled 2s extend from the back, and mid is the pointer actively sweeping and deciding each element's fate. None of them are fixed constants, running counters, or reserved only for output — they're all live boundaries that move during the algorithm.

mcqs.question: Why doesn't mid advance immediately after swapping arr[mid] with arr[high]?
options: Because the value swapped in from high is unknown and needs to be examined on the next iteration, unlike a swap with low where the incoming value is guaranteed to be a 1
Because high is always the last index and mid can never reach it
Because advancing mid after a high-swap would cause an index-out-of-bounds error
It's an arbitrary implementation choice with no effect on correctness
mcqs.explanation: The invariant guarantees the value pulled in from low is already a settled 1, so it's safe to skip past — but the value pulled in from high comes from the unprocessed zone and could be anything, so mid must examine it before moving on. This is required for correctness, not an arbitrary choice, and has nothing to do with array bounds.

mcqs.question: Comparing a count-then-rewrite approach to the one-pass Dutch flag algorithm for sorting 0/1/2, what's the actual difference between them?
options: Both are O(n) time and O(1) space; the difference is the number of passes over the array (two vs one), not the complexity class
The count-then-rewrite approach is O(n²) while the Dutch flag algorithm is O(n)
The Dutch flag algorithm uses O(n) extra space for its three markers, while counting uses O(1)
Only the Dutch flag algorithm can handle arrays containing duplicate values
mcqs.explanation: Both approaches are O(n) time and O(1) space — the Dutch flag algorithm's advantage is doing it in a single sweep rather than two, which is specifically what's being tested when an interviewer asks for a one-pass solution. Three index variables are O(1) space regardless, and both approaches handle duplicates fine since the whole problem is about duplicate values.

mcqs.question: A candidate writes mid += 1 unconditionally after every branch, including the swap with high. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing goes wrong — mid should always advance after any swap
The value just swapped in from high hasn't been checked yet, so skipping past it can leave the array incorrectly partitioned
The algorithm would crash with an index error on the next iteration
It only causes a problem when the array contains no 2s at all
mcqs.explanation: The value pulled in from high is from the unprocessed zone and could be a 0, 1, or 2 — advancing mid without examining it risks leaving that value unresolved and breaking the invariant, not a crash. This bug can slip through small test cases and doesn't depend on the array lacking 2s.

mcqs.question: You need to partition a list of (priority, task) pairs into three tiers while preserving each tier's original relative order. Does the Dutch flag partition satisfy that requirement as-is?
options: Yes — it's stable by construction since swaps only happen between elements in different regions
No — the partition isn't stable, so elements within the same tier can end up in a different relative order than they started in
Yes, but only if the array is sorted before partitioning
No — the partition can only be applied to arrays of exactly three distinct values
mcqs.explanation: Swapping elements unconditionally moves them without regard to original position, so two equal-tier elements can end up reordered relative to each other — this partition is not stable. It doesn't require pre-sorting, and it generalizes past exactly three values via the pivot-based version.

mcqs.question: A solution uses a standard two-pointer (two-way) partition instead of the three-marker Dutch flag technique on a 0/1/2 sorting problem. Why might this pass basic tests but fail a stricter requirement?
options: A two-way partition runs in O(n²) time, so it would simply time out on large inputs

A two-way partition has no distinct boundary for an equal/middle region, so it silently folds it into one of the two sides — fine for producing a sorted array, but broken if the three groups need to be reported separately
A two-way partition cannot be implemented in-place
A two-way partition only works when the array has no duplicate values
mcqs.explanation: A two-way partition can still produce a technically sorted 0/1/2 array by absorbing the middle group into one side, which is why casual tests can pass — but it has no marked boundary for that middle group, which breaks the moment the problem needs each bucket's range reported. Two-way partitions are commonly implemented in-place and run in O(n), and this problem is specifically about arrays full of duplicates.
